question: A tension load test on a 180 kg bridge component uses stress polynomial x² - 6x + 8, selecting the smaller root (2 m/s²). The acceleration is amplified 9 times to 18 m/s², applied to the mass for force calculation, converted to kN, increased by 13 kN for safety margin, then reduced by 2 kN for instrument offset. A calibration temperature of 20°C is noted but unused. What is the final applied tensile load in kN?

A rate function 5*x^2 is integrated from x = 0 to x = 2, yielding an acceleration in m/s^2. A 45 kg mass experiences this acceleration. The force is reduced by 14 newtons, scaled by 6, converted to kilonewtons, and 9 kilonewtons are subtracted. A distance of 500 meters was noted but does not factor in. What is the final force in kilonewtons?

A 172,000 g pallet on a warehouse lift is accelerated at a rate in m/s² equal to the larger root of x² - 9x + 18 = 0. The hoisting force needed for this is converted to kN. There are 7 lifts per building and 11 buildings, so the site figure is the per-lift value multiplied by 7 and then by 11. A 3 kN allowance is then added. What is the final figure, in kN?

A rail depot's shed figure is 11 times the force taken by a single bay, expressed in kilonewtons. A bay drives a wagon of mass 173 kg. The wagon's acceleration, in metres per second squared, is a meter total minus 5. That total is what the bay's meter accumulates between the 1st and the 4th second, where the meter's instantaneous rate at time t seconds is 2 times t squared plus 3 times t. The depot's inspection pit is 30 m long. What is the shed figure, in kN?

What the site engineer wants to know is how far the demand on a winch exceeds its 7 kN rating, in kilonewtons, with a negative answer meaning the winch is within its rating. The winch drags 5 identical crates, each of mass 85 kg, along a level ramp. Each crate accelerates at a rate in metres per second squared equal to the rate of change of 1x^3 - 4x^2 with respect to x at x = 4. Find the pull needed on one crate in newtons, multiply by 5 for all the crates, and convert the total to kilonewtons. Then subtract the 7 kN rating. What is the result in kN?
GCD: gcd(253, 338) = 1. A 174-kilogram system at 1 m/s² generates force. Convert to kilojoules, add 7, add 26, scale by 9. Buffer: 1MB, not needed. What is the force in kN?

A projectile's velocity is the larger root of x squared minus 14 times x plus 48 equals zero. A 50-kilogram projectile at this velocity develops kinetic energy as half mass times velocity squared. Multiply by 12, convert from Joules to kilojoules, multiply by 9, and add 2 kilojoules to find the impact energy. What is the impact energy in kilojoules?

Parameter x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0; smaller root. A 26-kilogram load at this velocity (in m/s) has energy. Subtract 8, add 6, scale by 10, convert to kilojoules. Trace: disabled, not needed. What is the energy in kJ?

A brick works drives a ram carrying a mass of 98 kg. The ram's position along its guide, in metres, is 2 times the cube of the elapsed seconds plus 0 times the square of the elapsed seconds, and the works takes how fast it is moving at the instant 1 second in as the acceleration in metres per second squared. Seven identical rams work each press, and the press log then adds 14 N for the ejector spring. The works operates 6 identical presses. What total force do the works' presses supply, in N?

On a lab test bench, two speeds, in m/s, sum to 10 and multiply to 21; the larger is kept as the speed of a 19 kg slider. From the slider's kinetic energy, 11 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 12, then 8 J is subtracted, and finally the result is scaled once more by a factor of 10. What is the final energy, in joules?

On a go-kart test track, acceleration follows a(t) = 2t² + t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 3 s and t = 4 s, from the area under this graph, belongs to a battery pack whose mass is stated as 24000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 10 J is added, and the total is converted into kilojoules. Finally, 15 kJ is added. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A rail depot wants the combined force, in kilonewtons, needed to start 9 identical model wagons at once. Each model wagon has a mass of 138 000 g. The wagons' acceleration, in m/s², is obtained by doubling the area under the curve y = 1·x² + 3x from x = 0 to x = 3 and then subtracting 15. What is the combined force, in kN?
The calculation 8*(2 + 5) = 56 m/s. A 46 kg mass has kinetic energy converted to kJ, scaled by 12, increased by 28, scaled by 5. A rating is 100 kJ. What is the final energy in kJ?

The number the log ends with is 12 times a figure that is 27 kJ above the kilojoule reading described below. A launch controller adds its two dial settings 2 and 1 and multiplies the sum by 8 to fix the release speed, in metres per second, of a sled whose mass is 10000 g. The sled runs on a level rail and the energy it carries because of its motion is recorded, and because 4 identical sleds are launched per run the run energy is 4 times that value. That run energy, expressed in kilojoules, is the reading in question. The rail is 14 m long. What number does the log end with, in kJ?

The very last adjustment on this rig's readout always adds 27 to the kilonewton value before it's recorded — remember that going in. A forklift's fork assembly has a mass of 30,000 grams, that is, 30 kilograms. Two positive numbers add up to 12 and multiply together to 32; take the smaller of the two as the fork assembly's acceleration, in meters per second squared, while lifting a pallet. That acceleration produces a lifting force, which is converted from newtons into kilonewtons. The warehouse runs 8 identical forklifts on that shift, so the reading is multiplied by 8, and then multiplied by 8 again because each forklift makes 8 lifts per hour. Finally, exactly as noted at the start, 27 is added. The warehouse ceiling is 9 meters high. What is the final value, in kilonewtons?

Two shaft encoders on a test rig cycle through 250 and 128 ticks per run. The largest whole number that divides evenly into both counts is the speed, in meters per second, of an 8,000 gram calibration puck. Find its kinetic energy, then multiply it by 12, by 4, by 9, and by 9 again in turn, representing four successive test-batch multipliers. A separate voltmeter nearby reads 128 volts, unrelated to this calculation. What is the final energy, in joules?

A quarry laboratory releases a runaway trolley down a sloped rail. The trolley's release speed v, in m/s, is the larger value that satisfies v^2 - 8v + 7 = 0. The trolley has a mass of 55000 g, and the rail is kept at 15 degrees C during the test. The energy the trolley carries by virtue of its motion at release is expressed in kilojoules, and the laboratory releases 3 identical trolleys in each test. A trigger spring contributes a further 1 kJ to the test's combined figure. The laboratory's fixed instrument allowance of 28 kJ is then subtracted. What is the laboratory's net figure, in kJ?

A robot arm on an assembly line moves a 25 kg gearbox casing along a 3 m guide. The casing accelerates at a rate in metres per second squared equal to the rate of change of the curve 5x^3 - 2x^2 with respect to x at x = 1. Find the force in newtons needed to accelerate the casing. The arm must also overcome 23 N of guide friction, so add 23 N, and a balance spring contributes 1 N, so subtract 1 N. Express the arm's required force in kilonewtons. What is it in kN?

A quadratic solver finds the smaller root of x² - 13x + 42 = 0 (which is 6 m/s²). A 93 kg mass yields force, increased by 17 N, scaled by 8, converted to kilonewtons, and scaled by 7. What is the final force in kiloNewtons?

A production cycle sums from 1 to 9, yielding 45. This total becomes the acceleration in m/s² for a 180 kg load. The resulting force is multiplied by 3 through the transmission. This force converts to kilonewtons. Subtracting 27 kN for baseline load gives an intermediate value. The result is amplified by 2 times for the design multiplier. What is the final design load in kN? (The cycle runs at 60 Hz, which is not relevant.)
Calculate 11 choose 2, yielding 55. A system with mass 22 kilograms has this acceleration. Calculate force. Add 13. Convert to kiloNewtons. Add 15. Scale by 6. What is the final force in kiloNewtons?

A trajectory 3x³ + 4x² has velocity (first derivative) at x = 2. A ball with mass 35 kilograms travels at this velocity. Calculate kinetic energy. Scale by 5. Add 17. Scale by 8. What is the final energy in Joules?

A calibration rig holds 13 identical reference masses, and the acceleration it applies, in metres per second squared, is the number of distinct pairs that can be chosen from them. That acceleration is given to a shuttle of 5000 grams on the rig's rail. The controller records the force needed to drive the shuttle and multiplies it by 3, because the routine runs on 3 axes, then expresses the result in kilonewtons. A fixed frame allowance of 21 kN is added to the converted figure, and the sum is multiplied by 2 because two rigs run the routine together. What number, in kilonewtons, does the controller report?

On a laboratory test track, a sled with a mass of 39000 g is held at rest until t = 1 s and then released, and from t = 1 s to t = 2 s its acceleration in m/s² follows 3t² + 8t, with t in seconds. The sled itself is 1.2 m long. At the instant t = 2 s a booster fires and multiplies the sled's speed by exactly 2. The engineer wants the energy the sled carries purely because of its motion right after the booster, but reduced by the 29 J that the rails have already turned into heat. What is that remaining energy, in kJ?

An equation x^2 - 13*x + 40 = 0 yields the smaller root as acceleration in m/s^2. An 82 kg mass experiences this acceleration. The force is scaled by 6, reduced by 4 newtons, and converted to kilonewtons, with 12 kilonewtons subtracted. A wind speed of 30 km/h was noted but is not needed. What is the final force in kilonewtons?
